EEG showed mid-to-late centro-temporal lateralization tied to reported selection side, with neural information predicting beyond acoustic asymmetry. Evaluation used mirror-constrained and pairing-held-out protocols against acoustic, EEG, and multimodal baselines with ablations.
AI.conclusion: Spontaneous auditory selection is computationally accounted for as an interaction between generalizable stimulus priority and trial-specific neural variability.

title: Fold'EM: Direct atomic structure inference from Cryo-EM particles
summary: Single-particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) has become a widely adopted technique for biomolecular structure determination. The conventional cryo-EM computational pipeline first combines many particle images to reconstruct an electrostatic potential (ESP) map and then fits an atomic model to the recovered map. Density reconstruction has high sample complexity, requiring large numbers of particle images and making structure determination high-cost and low-throughput, particularly for heterogeneous samples. Downstream atomic model building, in turn, becomes increasingly difficult as the resolution of the reconstructed map deteriorates. Protein structure prediction models provide strong sequence-derived priors on atomic structure, and experiment-guided approaches can use these priors to recover structures consistent with experimental measurements. Yet, in cryo-EM, such priors are typically integrated only after density reconstruction during atomic model fitting. We introduce Fold'EM, an inference-time framework that combines priors from protein generative models directly with cryo-EM particle images to determine atomic models from a small number of single particle images, bypassing both intermediate density reconstruction and downstream model building against the reconstructed map. Across synthetic and experimental cryo-EM datasets, Fold'EM recovers accurate atomic structures both with known particle orientations and in an ab-initio setting where orientations are inferred jointly with structure. In heterogeneous datasets, Fold'EM further resolves distinct conformational states from mixed particle populations without separately reconstructing a density map and building an atomic model for each state. We believe these results open new avenues for structure determination in the low-sample regime and for characterizing low-population conformational states directly from cryo-EM particles.

AI.tldr: Fold'EM combines protein generative model priors directly with cryo-EM particle images at inference time, bypassing density reconstruction and model fitting to determine atomic structures from few particle images.
AI.motivation: Conventional cryo-EM pipelines have high sample complexity: they reconstruct an ESP map from many images, then fit an atomic model, making it costly and low-throughput, especially for heterogeneous samples. Protein structure priors are typically only used after density reconstruction, missing the chance to guide it.
AI.method: Fold'EM is an inference-time framework that integrates priors from protein generative models directly with cryo-EM particle images, avoiding intermediate density reconstruction and downstream model building against a reconstructed map.
AI.result: On synthetic and experimental cryo-EM datasets, Fold'EM recovers accurate atomic structures with known particle orientations and in an ab-initio setting where orientations are jointly inferred. It also resolves distinct conformational states from mixed populations without separate per-state density reconstruction and model building.
AI.conclusion: These results open new avenues for structure determination in the low-sample regime and for characterizing low-population conformational states directly from cryo-EM particles.

title: CPathOGen: Spatially and Morphologically Controlled H&E Counterfactuals for Probing Pathology Models
summary: Computational pathology models infer biologically and clinically meaningful outcomes from histology, but their predictions are shaped by complex, intertwined tissue signals whose roles are important to understand. Common pixel- and feature-space perturbations can produce implausible tissue, making model responses difficult to interpret. We introduce CPathOGen, a conditional latent-diffusion framework for generating paired H\&E counterfactuals with explicit controls over cellular spatial organization, nuclear morphology, and stain appearance. Cellular maps condition spatial structure through a spatial encoder, while a morphology/appearance vector modulates denoising through blockwise feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM). On held-out H\&E tiles, CPathOGen generates visually plausible tissue with improved distributional agreement after spatially guided selection, as reflected by lower Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) and Kernel Inception Distance (KID); generated cells track requested abundance and position, and measured morphology and color vary monotonically with their controls. We use these verified interventions to probe pathology encoders with endpoint heads, task-specific classifiers, and survival models. Responses are quantified using total variation distance and prediction-flip rate. We further introduce the Biology-Nuisance Sensitivity Ratio, a metric that contrasts model sensitivity to biologically motivated morphology and spatial factors with sensitivity to non-biological, stain-related nuisance variation. CPathOGen provides a practical, fidelity-audited framework for evaluating robustness and controlled feature sensitivity in computational pathology model. \href{https://github.com/a12dongithub/PathOGen}{GitHub} and \href{https://huggingface.co/a12donhf/CPathOGen}{Hugging~Face}.

AI.tldr: CPathOGen is a conditional latent-diffusion framework that generates paired H&E counterfactuals with explicit control over cellular spatial organization, nuclear morphology, and stain appearance, enabling fidelity-audited robustness and feature-sensitivity evaluation of computational pathology models.
AI.motivation: Computational pathology models infer meaningful outcomes from histology, but their predictions are shaped by complex, intertwined tissue signals. Common pixel- and feature-space perturbations produce implausible tissue, making model responses difficult to interpret.
AI.method: A conditional latent-diffusion framework generating paired H&E counterfactuals. Cellular maps condition spatial structure via a spatial encoder; a morphology/appearance vector modulates denoising through blockwise FiLM. Interventions are verified and used to probe pathology encoders with endpoint heads, task-specific classifiers, and survival models.
AI.result: On held-out H&E tiles, CPathOGen generates visually plausible tissue with lower FID and KID after spatially guided selection; generated cells track requested abundance and position, and measured morphology/color vary monotonically with controls. Model responses are quantified via total variation distance and prediction-flip rate, plus a new Biology-Nuisance Sensitivity Ratio.
AI.conclusion: CPathOGen provides a practical, fidelity-audited framework for evaluating robustness and controlled feature sensitivity in computational pathology models. Code and models are publicly released.

title: Analysis of Quantized and Efficiently Adapted Protein Language Models
summary: Background: Protein language models (PLMs) are increasingly used for sequence generation and property prediction, but their size makes fine-tuning and deployment expensive. The effects of quantization and parameter efficient fine-tuning on performance, representations and generation remain insufficiently characterized. Results: We evaluated 4-bit quantization and low-rank adapter fine-tuning (QLoRA) across ESM-2, ESMC, ProtBERT, ProtT5, Ankh, Ankh3 and Profluent-E1. Across protein prediction tasks, many model-task pairs retained more than 90% of full fine-tuning performance. Peak GPU memory savings approached 90% for the largest models, although performance and efficiency varied by model, dataset and training configuration. QLoRA often preserved early-layer representations while inducing task-specific adaptations in middle and late layers, resembling full fine-tuning with smaller representational changes. Training speed and power effects were more varied. For unconditional generation with ProLLaMA, ProtGPT2, ProGen2, ProteinGLM and ESM3, 4-bit quantization largely preserved predicted structural and sequence-level properties, but token-level analysis revealed model-dependent shifts in autoregressive output distributions. Conclusion: QLoRA and 4-bit quantization reduce PLM computational requirements, particularly GPU memory usage. Our results support QLoRA as a first-pass strategy for memory limited adaptation, reserving full fine-tuning for challenging tasks, unstable architectures or low validation recovery. For generative PLMs, sequence-level and structural metrics should be complemented with distributional analysis, since downstream predictions alone may miss quantization-induced shifts. These approaches can broaden access to large-scale protein modelling while requiring model- and task-specific validation.

AI.tldr: This study evaluates 4-bit quantization and QLoRA across seven protein language models, showing substantial GPU memory savings (up to ~90%) while often retaining >90% of full fine-tuning performance, with model/task-dependent representational and generative shifts.
AI.motivation: PLMs are increasingly used for sequence generation and property prediction, but their large size makes fine-tuning and deployment expensive. The effects of quantization and parameter-efficient fine-tuning on performance, representations, and generation remain insufficiently characterized.
AI.method: Evaluated 4-bit quantization and low-rank adapter fine-tuning (QLoRA) across ESM-2, ESMC, ProtBERT, ProtT5, Ankh, Ankh3 and Profluent-E1 for prediction tasks, and analyzed unconditional generation with ProLLaMA, ProtGPT2, ProGen2, ProteinGLM and ESM3, including representational and token-level distributional analysis.
AI.result: Many model-task pairs retained >90% of full fine-tuning performance; peak GPU memory savings approached 90% for the largest models, though performance and efficiency varied by model, dataset and training configuration. QLoRA often preserved early-layer representations while inducing task-specific adaptations in middle and late layers. For generation, 4-bit quantization largely preserved structural and sequence-level properties, but token-level analysis revealed model-dependent shifts in autoregressive output distributions.
AI.conclusion: QLoRA and 4-bit quantization reduce PLM computational requirements, especially GPU memory. QLoRA is supported as a first-pass strategy for memory-limited adaptation, reserving full fine-tuning for challenging tasks, unstable architectures, or low validation recovery. For generative PLMs, sequence-level and structural metrics should be complemented with distributional analysis, since downstream predictions alone may miss quantization-induced shifts.

title: ORBIT-FMIB: Tracking Order-Resolved Epistatic Information Through ESM-2
summary:
Protein foundation models support mutation-effect and structural prediction, but predictive performance alone does not reveal which forms of biological interaction information remain accessible through model depth. We ask whether ESM-2 retains higher-order epistatic information as strongly as first- and second-order information across its representation hierarchy, introducing ORBIT-FMIB, a diagnostic framework combining Walsh-based interaction decomposition with subset-conditioned neural dependence estimation. The method is validated on synthetic landscapes with known interaction structure before being applied to the dense four-site GB1 fitness landscape using frozen ESM-2 representations.
  An initial production run suggested ESM-2 retains higher-order epistatic information less well than lower-order information ($Δ_{\mathrm{HO-LO}}=-0.107$). An independent replication of the complete measurement grid, under matched GPU hardware and identical critic seeds, substantially reduced this contrast ($Δ_{\mathrm{HO-LO}}=-0.017$), and its sign was unstable across otherwise-defensible evaluation-pairing choices applied to the same trained critics ($-0.011$ to $+0.015$). We therefore do not currently have robust evidence that ESM-2 selectively loses higher-order epistatic information, nor that retention is equal across orders; the directional question remains open. The measurement protocol itself, including its documented removal of a positional-subset shortcut in pooled critics, remains validated and is unaffected by this finding. ORBIT-FMIB is offered as a diagnostic framework for probing interaction structure in protein foundation models; this study's own replication result illustrates why such probing requires adequately-powered reproducibility checks before its output is treated as a biological finding.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ORBIT-FMIB, a diagnostic framework to test whether ESM-2 preserves higher-order epistatic information across its layers, but a replication of its own experiment undercuts the initial finding: the claimed loss of higher-order information is not robustly reproducible, leaving the directional question open.
AI.motivation: Protein foundation models are used for mutation-effect and structural prediction, yet strong predictive performance does not indicate what kind of biological interaction information (first-, second-, or higher-order epistasis) is actually encoded in a model's internal representations. The authors want to determine whether ESM-2 retains higher-order epistatic information as well as lower-order information.
AI.method: ORBIT-FMIB combines Walsh-based interaction decomposition with subset-conditioned neural dependence estimation. It is validated on synthetic fitness landscapes with known interaction structure, then applied to the dense four-site GB1 fitness landscape using frozen ESM-2 representations. An independent replication of the full measurement grid was run under matched GPU hardware and identical critic seeds, and the sign of the effect was tested across alternative evaluation-pairing choices applied to the same trained critics.
AI.result: The initial production run suggested ESM-2 retains higher-order epistatic information poorly (Δ_HO-LO = -0.107). The independent replication reduced this contrast to Δ_HO-LO = -0.017, and the sign was unstable across defensible evaluation-pairing choices (-0.011 to +0.015). Thus there is no robust evidence that ESM-2 selectively loses higher-order epistatic information, nor that retention is equal across orders.
AI.conclusion: The directional question about order-dependent information retention in ESM-2 remains open. The measurement protocol itself, including its removal of a positional-subset shortcut in pooled critics, remains validated and unaffected. ORBIT-FMIB is offered as a diagnostic framework for probing interaction structure in protein foundation models, and the study's own replication illustrates why such probing needs adequately-powered reproducibility checks before output is treated as a biological finding.

title: Neuromorphic Pseudo-Random Number Generators with a Low Power Hardware Implementation
summary: Pseudo-random number generation often requires trade-offs among quality, power consumption, and bandwidth to produce unpredictable sequences of numbers. The brain, on the other hand, efficiently generates unpredictable output complex network dynamics occurring in a high-dimensional state. This state, which is hypothesized to be chaotic, relies on the balance between excitation and inhibition. Here, we investigated if computational models of these chaotic balanced states can be harnessed for Neuromorphic Pseudo-Random Number Generators (NPRNGs) in low power hardware. We successfully constructed a balanced spiking neural network model consisting of leaky-integrate-and-fire neurons that could be readily implemented in low power FPGAs and used as a NPRNG. The prototyped NPRNG consumed 3.24 mW during operation and produced pseudo-random numbers at 120kbps. In both hardware and software instantiations, NPRNGs produce high-quality random numbers as validated by standard metrics for testing RNG quality.

AI.tldr: A balanced spiking neural network with chaotic dynamics is prototyped on FPGA as a low-power neuromorphic pseudo-random number generator (NPRNG), consuming 3.24 mW at 120 kbps while producing high-quality random numbers.
AI.motivation: Pseudo-random number generation traditionally involves trade-offs among quality, power consumption, and bandwidth. Inspired by the brain's efficient generation of unpredictable output via chaotic, high-dimensional network dynamics reliant on excitation-inhibition balance, the authors explore whether such balanced chaotic states can be leveraged for low-power neuromorphic RNGs.
AI.method: The authors constructed a balanced spiking neural network model of leaky-integrate-and-fire neurons exhibiting chaotic balanced dynamics. This model was implemented in software and on low-power FPGA hardware as an NPRNG.
AI.result: The prototyped NPRNG consumed 3.24 mW during operation and generated pseudo-random numbers at 120 kbps. Both hardware and software instantiations produced high-quality random numbers, validated by standard RNG quality metrics.
AI.conclusion: Computational models of chaotic balanced neural states can be successfully harnessed for low-power neuromorphic pseudo-random number generation, achieving competitive power-bandwidth performance with high randomness quality.

title: Increasing Width Allows Greedy Layer-wise Training to Rival End-to-End Backpropagation in Self-Supervised Learning
summary: End-to-end backpropagation has been the dominant mode of training in deep learning, allowing for the coordination of parameter updates across layers of a neural network. Prior studies have explored alternative -- and, in some cases, simpler -- training mechanisms, showing that they can sometimes achieve performance similar to backpropagation. However, the architectural conditions under which locally optimized networks, which avoid end-to-end backpropagation of error, can learn representations comparable to those learned through end-to-end training remain unclear. We aim to answer this question in the context of self-supervised learning, an important framework for large-scale pretraining in artificial intelligence. Here, we investigate how network width and depth affect the efficacy of greedy layer-wise and end-to-end self-supervised training in convolutional networks. We find that in wider networks, the benefits of end-to-end backpropagation over greedy layer-wise training shrink: in relatively shallow and very wide networks, we even observed higher performance in models trained with greedy layer-wise training. Subsequent analysis of the representations formed by these networks shows that very wide greedy-trained networks exhibit more favorable representational geometry than do networks trained end-to-end with backpropagation. This work shows that width can compensate for restricted credit assignment and identifies differences in representational geometry as a potential mechanism for their improved performance.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how network width and depth affect the efficacy of greedy layer-wise versus end-to-end self-supervised training in convolutional networks, finding that wider networks reduce the gap between the two, with very wide and relatively shallow greedy-trained networks even outperforming end-to-end models due to more favorable representational geometry.
AI.motivation: End-to-end backpropagation dominates deep learning, but it remains unclear under what architectural conditions locally optimized (non-end-to-end) networks can learn representations comparable to end-to-end training. This is especially relevant for self-supervised learning used in large-scale pretraining.
AI.method: The authors compare greedy layer-wise and end-to-end self-supervised training in convolutional networks, systematically varying network width and depth, and then analyze the representational geometry of the resulting networks.
AI.result: In wider networks the benefits of end-to-end backpropagation over greedy layer-wise training shrink, and in relatively shallow yet very wide networks greedy layer-wise training even achieved higher performance. Analysis showed very wide greedy-trained networks form more favorable representational geometry than end-to-end backpropagation-trained networks.
AI.conclusion: Network width can compensate for restricted credit assignment, and differences in representational geometry are identified as a potential mechanism underlying the improved performance of greedy layer-wise trained wide networks.

title: MorphoBranch: A Fine-Structure-Preserving Workbench for Morphometric Analysis of Branched Cellular Structures
summary: Background and Objectives: Fluorescence-labeled cellular arbors provide readouts of neuronal and microglial morphology, but fine and weakly labeled processes are prone to fragmentation and false connections that bias skeleton-based measurements. We present MorphoBranch, a fine-structure-preserving, human-reviewable workbench for morphometry of branched cellular structures. Methods: MorphoBranch combines a deterministic Morphometry Engine with an LLM-assisted Refinement Engine. The Mor- phometry Engine implements an image-to-graph workflow integrating multiscale structural evidence extraction, hysteresis segmen- tation, evidence-constrained skeleton refinement, and graph-based morphometry. The Refinement Engine maps natural-language requests to registered actions for parameter adjustment, preview execution, metric reporting, and unsupported-request handling, while image processing and quantitative computation remain deterministic and reviewable. Results: MorphoBranch was evaluated on two public neuronal axon datasets, AxonMIP and AxonStack, and the in-house Cell- Morph dataset of microglial fluorescence images. It achieved the highest Skeleton F1 and clDice and the lowest length-estimation error among the evaluated methods on all three datasets, while also achieving the highest Dice and IoU on AxonMIP and Axon- Stack. Across 150 natural-language tasks, the Refinement Engine achieved a 94.0% end-to-end success rate. Conclusions: These results demonstrate that MorphoBranch provides a reproducible, human-reviewable workflow for mor- phometric analysis of branched cellular structures. It supports fine-structure-preserving quantification across neuronal axon and microglial fluorescence images while maintaining inspectable and reproducible analysis workflows.

AI.tldr: MorphoBranch is a human-reviewable workbench combining a deterministic Morphometry Engine with an LLM-assisted Refinement Engine for fine-structure-preserving morphometry of branched cellular structures, achieving top skeleton-based metrics across neuronal and microglial datasets.
AI.motivation: Fluorescence-labeled cellular arbors reveal neuronal and microglial morphology, but fine and weakly labeled processes fragment and form false connections, biasing skeleton-based measurements. Existing morphometry tools lack fine-structure preservation and human-reviewable, reproducible workflows.
AI.method: MorphoBranch pairs a deterministic Morphometry Engine (image-to-graph workflow with multiscale structural evidence extraction, hysteresis segmentation, evidence-constrained skeleton refinement, and graph-based morphometry) with an LLM-assisted Refinement Engine that maps natural-language requests to registered actions (parameter adjustment, preview, metric reporting, unsupported-request handling) while keeping image processing and computation deterministic.
AI.result: On AxonMIP, AxonStack, and the in-house CellMorph microglial dataset, MorphoBranch achieved the highest Skeleton F1 and clDice and lowest length-estimation error across all three datasets, plus the highest Dice and IoU on AxonMIP and AxonStack. The Refinement Engine reached 94.0% end-to-end success across 150 natural-language tasks.
AI.conclusion: MorphoBranch delivers a reproducible, human-reviewable workflow for morphometric analysis of branched cellular structures, supporting fine-structure-preserving quantification of neuronal axon and microglial fluorescence images with inspectable, reproducible analysis.

title: Efficient Convex Optimization Methods for State-Space Heartbeat Dynamics Models with Gamma Generalized Linear Models
summary: Objective: This work proposes a dynamic state-space statistical model of heartbeat dynamics whose optimal state estimate can be solved efficiently with convex optimization and used to assess autonomic and cardiovascular health. Methods: This state-space model combines a Gauss-Markov process prior with gamma emissions using a log-link function. Parameters are estimated using a static version of the model, and alternating direction method of multipliers is used to efficiently find the optimal maximum a priori latent state estimate. Model selection is performed by finding the tradeoff between model size and model fit using the partial autocorrelation function. Results: We demonstrate in synthetically generated heartbeats that this model is able to closely recover the underlying latent weights. Then, we show using a tilt table dataset that this statistical model is able to better capture sharp transients in heart rate patterns than traditional local averaging methods. In addition, combining heart beat timings with information from other organs such as the respiratory phase, we show that our statistical modeling framework enables the extraction of information-theoretic measures to quantify inter-organ coupling such as respiratory sinus arrythmia. Conclusion: This statistical framework for modeling heartbeat dynamics provides an efficient framework that can provide physiologically meaningful insights. Significance: This work broadens potential tools that can be used to assess heartbeat dynamics.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a dynamic state-space statistical model of heartbeat dynamics, solved efficiently via convex optimization, for assessing autonomic and cardiovascular health.
AI.motivation: Traditional local averaging methods fail to capture sharp transients in heart rate patterns, limiting physiologically meaningful assessment of heartbeat dynamics.
AI.method: A state-space model combining a Gauss-Markov process prior with gamma emissions via a log-link function. Parameters are estimated from a static version, and ADMM efficiently computes the optimal maximum a priori latent state estimate. Model selection trades off size vs. fit using the partial autocorrelation function.
AI.result: On synthetic heartbeats the model closely recovers latent weights. On a tilt table dataset it better captures sharp heart rate transients than local averaging. Combining heartbeat timings with respiratory phase enables information-theoretic measures of inter-organ coupling such as respiratory sinus arrhythmia.
AI.conclusion: The framework offers an efficient, physiologically meaningful way to model heartbeat dynamics, broadening tools for assessing autonomic and cardiovascular health.

title: Auditable Algebraic Counting Field for Cryptic-Pocket Detection from Apo Structures
comment: Accepted for publication in Pacific Symposium on Biocomputing (PSB) 2027
summary: Cryptic ligand-binding pockets are not apparent in experimentally determined apo structures, making them difficult to identify from unbound receptor geometry. A complementary challenge is to make the structural measurements and learned evidence behind each prediction directly inspectable. We introduce a supervised algebraic counting field (ACF) for predicting cryptic-pocket residues from apo structures. ACF compiles explicit geometric, physicochemical, and topological features into compact, integer-weighted lookup tables. Each prediction score can be reconstructed from feature values, training counts, table weights, and spatial aggregation, without sequence search, structural-template transfer, or a protein language model at inference. We evaluate ACF on CryptoBench and two locked external collections, separating ranking performance from the effects of residue-calling budgets. On an external set of 57 post-CryptoBench apo-holo units, ACF exceeded P2Rank by +0.044 in mean paired ROC-AUC (multiplicity-adjusted 95% CI [+0.010, +0.079]). The advantage was dataset-dependent: official-fold ROC-AUC and matched-budget F1 differences against P2Rank remained unresolved, and a second external evaluation did not confirm gains from added structural features. ACF thus provides a compact predictor with externally validated signal and an inspectable path from structural measurements and training counts to residue scores.

AI.tldr: ACF, a supervised algebraic counting field using integer-weighted lookup tables of geometric, physicochemical, and topological features, predicts cryptic-pocket residues from apo structures with inspectable, externally validated signal beating P2Rank on one external set.
AI.motivation: Cryptic ligand-binding pockets are not visible in apo structures, making them hard to identify from unbound receptor geometry. Additionally, existing predictions are often not directly inspectable—the structural measurements and learned evidence behind each prediction cannot be easily traced.
AI.method: The authors introduce a supervised algebraic counting field (ACF) that compiles explicit geometric, physicochemical, and topological features into compact integer-weighted lookup tables. Each prediction score is reconstructible from feature values, training counts, table weights, and spatial aggregation, without sequence search, structural-template transfer, or a protein language model at inference.
AI.result: Evaluated on CryptoBench and two locked external collections, separating ranking from residue-calling budgets. On 57 post-CryptoBench apo-holo units, ACF exceeded P2Rank by +0.044 in mean paired ROC-AUC (95% CI [+0.010, +0.079]). However, the advantage was dataset-dependent: official-fold ROC-AUC and matched-budget F1 differences versus P2Rank were unresolved, and a second external evaluation did not confirm gains from added structural features.
AI.conclusion: ACF provides a compact, inspectable predictor with externally validated signal, offering a transparent path from structural measurements and training counts to residue scores, though its advantage over P2Rank is dataset-dependent and not uniformly confirmed.

title: Selection rules for the harmonic spectroscopy of animal decisions
summary: Spectroscopy reads structure by sending a structured probe into a system and measuring what comes back. Here we apply this principle to animal decision-making. Harmonic Theory casts choice as motion on an angular landscape over heading, whose Fourier components form an animal's decision spectrum. We show that the arrangement of cues enters that landscape as a structure factor, so it factors like a diffraction amplitude, and symmetry imposes selection rules: a p-fold cue array annihilates every harmonic that is not a multiple of p, and sweeping two cues apart draws a notch through each harmonic. Cue geometry becomes a tunable probe: the experimenter sets which harmonics an experiment can see. We read these spectra from public recordings of flies, schooling fish, larval zebrafish, mice and a swimming alga, and from the fly's neural compass, where symmetric scenes suppress the forbidden harmonics and breaking that symmetry restores them. Measuring the compass form factor favours the theory's smooth bump over its square one, and raising cue contrast narrows that bump in every fly. A width fitted to one harmonic then predicts the next. Cue geometry is a spectrometer for decisions, and symmetry sets what it can see.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "Harmonic Theory," framing animal decision-making as motion on an angular landscape whose Fourier components form a decision spectrum. Cue arrangement acts as a structure factor with symmetry-imposed selection rules, letting cue geometry serve as a tunable spectrometer for reading decision spectra across diverse species and neural compass.
AI.motivation: Spectroscopy reads structure by probing a system and measuring the response. The authors aim to apply this principle to animal decision-making, providing a framework to understand how cue geometry shapes which decision features an experiment can observe.
AI.method: They cast choice as motion on an angular landscape over heading, whose Fourier components define a decision spectrum. Cue arrangement enters as a structure factor with diffraction-like symmetry selection rules (a p-fold cue array annihilates non-multiple-p harmonics). They read spectra from public recordings of flies, schooling fish, larval zebrafish, mice, and a swimming alga, plus the fly neural compass, and fit bump shapes to compass form factors.
AI.result: Symmetric scenes suppress forbidden harmonics while symmetry breaking restores them. Compass measurements favor a smooth bump over a square one, and raising cue contrast narrows the bump in every fly. A width fitted to one harmonic predicts the next.
AI.conclusion: Cue geometry functions as a spectrometer for decisions, and symmetry sets what it can see, offering a unifying, testable framework for animal decision-making across species and neural systems.

title: Compartmental epidemiological models with infection-driven immune escape
summary: We propose and study a compartmental epidemiological model that incorporates both waning immunity and mutation-driven immune escape into a single-strain framework. The model, termed SIRCm, extends the SIRC (Susceptible-Infected-Recovered-Cross-immune) model, in which recovered individuals pass through an intermediate cross-immune class before returning to full susceptibility. In SIRCm, both the rate of immune waning and the rate of immune escape are amplified by a feedback function tied to the current level of infection. We study two formulations of this feedback, a transmission-driven model, in which mutation opportunities arise at the point of new infection, and a prevalence-driven model, in which they arise in proportion to the infected population alone. For both models and any feedback strength, we prove existence of an endemic equilibrium using persistence theory, and characterize its behavior analytically in the weak and strong-feedback limits, recovering the SIRC and SIS models, respectively, as limiting cases. Unlike the SIRC model, we show that the SIRCm endemic equilibrium is unstable in certain parameter regimes. This leads to novel behavior, even in the absence of seasonal forcing.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the SIRCm compartmental model, combining waning immunity and mutation-driven immune escape within a single-strain framework, and analyzes its endemic equilibria and stability.
AI.motivation: Existing SIRC-type models capture waning immunity but not mutation-driven immune escape feedback; the paper aims to unify these within one framework to study emergent dynamics.
AI.method: Extends the SIRC model by amplifying waning and escape rates via a feedback function tied to infection level. Two variants: transmission-driven (mutation at new infection) and prevalence-driven (proportional to infected population). Uses persistence theory to prove endemic equilibrium existence and analyzes weak/strong-feedback limits.
AI.result: Proves existence of an endemic equilibrium for both models at any feedback strength. Recovers SIRC and SIS as limiting cases. Shows the SIRCm endemic equilibrium is unstable in certain parameter regimes.
AI.conclusion: Immune escape feedback can destabilize the endemic equilibrium, producing novel dynamics even without seasonal forcing, unlike the original SIRC model.

title: Can LLMs Reliably Annotate Bioassay Metadata to Improve Data Readiness?
comment: Accepted to the AIDaR workshop at NeurIPS
summary: The emergence of foundation models for molecular property prediction requires a high degree of AI data readiness, including reliable metadata annotation. However, both public repositories and industrial screening databases suffer from missing, inconsistent, or conflated assay annotations. In this work, we quantify the extent of missing annotations in PubChem for the BioAssay Ontology (BAO) assay format and physical detection method fields and investigate whether open-source and proprietary large language models (LLMs) can reliably predict and audit metadata annotations directly from the assay text. In our assessment, we found that the annotation coverage across PubChem's $\sim$2 million bioassays is critically sparse, 36\% lacking an assay format, 89\% a BioAssay type, and >99.9\% any BAO-mapped assay format or detection technology term. This motivates the need for automated test-metadata curation. Using evaluation sets derived from PubChem and ChEMBL, we assess the agreement of seven open-source and proprietary LLMs with existing silver labels. Recall is at least 0.96 for biochemical and cell-based assay formats, with a similar pattern for detection technology, although disagreements increase on under-represented classes. Manual inspection shows that many of these disagreements trace back to inconsistencies between silver sources rather than to LLM error. Moreover, in a qualitative study with a senior industrial curator, LLM-generated evidence prompted the expert to revise some of their own labels, showing LLMs can flag potentially mislabeled assays. Across the study, performance differences between proprietary and open-source models were small. Together, these results suggest LLMs can support the large-scale annotation and auditing of assay metadata, though per-class reliability estimates and targeted human review remain necessary before such labels enter downstream ML pipelines.

AI.tldr: This paper quantifies severe missing assay annotations in PubChem and evaluates whether LLMs can reliably predict and audit assay metadata from text, finding high recall and small open-vs-proprietary gaps.
AI.motivation: Foundation models for molecular property prediction need AI-ready data with reliable metadata annotation, yet public repositories and industrial screening databases suffer from missing, inconsistent, or conflated assay annotations.
AI.method: Quantified missing annotations in PubChem for BioAssay Ontology assay format and physical detection method fields; assessed seven open-source and proprietary LLMs in predicting and auditing metadata from assay text using evaluation sets derived from PubChem and ChEMBL, plus a qualitative study with a senior industrial curator.
AI.result: Annotation coverage across ~2 million PubChem bioassays is critically sparse: 36% lack an assay format, 89% a BioAssay type, and >99.9% any BAO-mapped assay format or detection technology term. Recall ≥0.96 for biochemical and cell-based formats and similar for detection technology, with more disagreements on under-represented classes; many disagreements reflect silver-source inconsistencies rather than LLM error, and LLM-generated evidence prompted an expert to revise some labels. Differences between proprietary and open-source models were small.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can support large-scale annotation and auditing of assay metadata, but per-class reliability estimates and targeted human review remain necessary before such labels enter downstream ML pipelines.

title: Autocatalysis and Boundary Stability in Chemical Reaction Systems
summary: The next-generation matrix method is a powerful tool for computing the basic reproduction number in compartmental mathematical models of infectious diseases. The method has been recently extended to mathematical biochemistry, where it can be used to establish parameter regions of stability and instability for boundary steady states. Several significant challenges in its application remain, however, particularly around establishing conditions under which the method is mathematically valid, computationally tractable, and biologically meaningful in the biochemical setting. In this paper, we address these challenges by shifting the interpretation from new infections in the epidemiological setting to autocatalysis in the biochemical setting. We introduce a graph, called the ALT-graph (autocatalysis-leak-transition graph), which decomposes the contribution of each reaction to the Jacobian as autocatalytic, leak, or transition edges. We then present a systematic algorithm for splitting the ALT-graph, which is guaranteed to produce a valid reproduction number, $ρ(FV^{-1})$, while also decreasing computational complexity by lowering the rank of $FV^{-1}$. We apply the method to models of both biochemical reaction networks and infectious disease spread.

AI.tldr: The paper extends the next-generation matrix method to biochemistry by reinterpreting "new infections" as autocatalysis, introducing the ALT-graph and a splitting algorithm to guarantee a valid, tractable, and biologically meaningful reproduction number.
AI.motivation: The next-generation matrix method is powerful for computing the basic reproduction number in epidemiological models and was recently extended to mathematical biochemistry to determine stability/instability regions of boundary steady states. However, challenges remain in ensuring the method is mathematically valid, computationally tractable, and biologically meaningful in the biochemical setting.
AI.method: The authors shift the interpretation from new infections (epidemiology) to autocatalysis (biochemistry). They introduce the ALT-graph (autocatalysis-leak-transition graph), which decomposes each reaction's contribution to the Jacobian into autocatalytic, leak, or transition edges, and present a systematic algorithm for splitting the ALT-graph.
AI.result: The splitting algorithm is guaranteed to produce a valid reproduction number, ρ(FV^{-1}), while reducing computational complexity by lowering the rank of FV^{-1}. The method is applied to models of both biochemical reaction networks and infectious disease spread.
AI.conclusion: By reinterpreting the next-generation matrix method through autocatalysis and the ALT-graph, the approach provides a valid, computationally efficient, and biologically meaningful framework, applicable across biochemical and epidemiological models.

title: pCoMole: Pareto-Constrained Molecule Editing with Discrete Flows
comment: Published at NeurIPS 2026. (Proceedings of the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems, Sydney, Australia)
summary: Biomolecular therapeutics often start from known sequences and require targeted editing to improve multiple properties while satisfying hard biochemical and manufacturability constraints. However, existing generative methods do not jointly support multi-objective optimization, hard feasibility, and sequence editing in discrete, variable-length biological spaces. In this work, we introduce Pareto-Constrained Molecule Editing (pCoMole), a framework built on discrete flow matching that steers a pre-trained Edit Flow toward user-specified preferences while enforcing terminal feasibility. pCoMole defines a feasibility-gated terminal distribution using an augmented Tchebycheff utility and realizes the resulting preference tilt through a Doob-h transform of the underlying edit process. To make this construction practical, we approximate the required harmonic function using short Monte Carlo rollouts over candidate edits, yielding an efficient guided editor with provable preference consistency. We validate pCoMole by shrinking GFP while retaining fluorescence-related properties, shortening diverse Cas9 orthologs while preserving PAM specificity, and compressing peptide binders into short peptidomimetics that optimize seven drug-related properties under hard constraints. In wet lab testing, two 229-residue pCoMole-designed eGFP variants retained clear green fluorescence in BL21 cells after 10 deletions, with either one or two substitutions. Together, pCoMole enables constraint-aware, Pareto-aligned editing of biomolecular sequences in discrete, variable-length spaces.

AI.tldr: pCoMole is a discrete flow matching framework for multi-objective, constraint-aware editing of biomolecular sequences that steers a pre-trained Edit Flow toward user preferences while enforcing terminal feasibility.
AI.motivation: Biomolecular therapeutics start from known sequences and need targeted editing to improve multiple properties under hard biochemical and manufacturability constraints, but existing generative methods cannot jointly handle multi-objective optimization, hard feasibility, and sequence editing in discrete, variable-length biological spaces.
AI.method: Built on discrete flow matching, pCoMole steers a pre-trained Edit Flow. It defines a feasibility-gated terminal distribution via an augmented Tchebycheff utility and realizes the preference tilt through a Doob-h transform of the edit process. The harmonic function is approximated with short Monte Carlo rollouts over candidate edits, giving an efficient guided editor with provable preference consistency.

AI.conclusion: pCoMole enables constraint-aware, Pareto-aligned editing of biomolecular sequences in discrete, variable-length spaces.

title: Inferring Multi-Timescale Neural Dynamics with Switching Linear Dynamical Systems
summary: Neural activity often exhibits multiple timescales that can vary with behavioral states and task conditions. Identifying these timescales from neural recordings is important for better understanding neural computation and function. However, traditional approaches based on autocorrelation fitting are difficult to scale to high-dimensional population recordings and can become unreliable when neural dynamics change with behavior. State-space models have been a powerful framework for modeling high-dimensional neural population activity through latent dynamical systems, but standard formulations and inference methods do not explicitly account for multiple timescales and therefore do not guarantee accurate recovery of the underlying temporal structure. Motivated by these questions, we introduce the Multi-Timescale Switching Linear Dynamical System (MTS-SLDS), a framework for identifying regime-specific latent timescales from continuous or spiking neural observations. MTS-SLDS combines a multi-lag moment initialization, which captures temporal structure across multiple observation lags, with \textit{regime-conditioned} Laplace-EM inference, which reduces mixing of dynamical statistics across uncertain regimes. Characteristic timescales can then be extracted directly from the eigenvalues of the learned latent transition matrices. In synthetic and neural experiments with Gaussian and Poisson spike observations, MTS-SLDS accurately recovers timescales and switching structure over multiple datasets.

AI.tldr: MTS-SLDS identifies regime-specific neural timescales by combining multi-lag moment initialization with regime-conditioned Laplace-EM inference in a switching linear dynamical system; it recovers timescales and switching structure in synthetic and neural data.
AI.motivation: Neural activity has multiple timescales that vary with behavior and task. Traditional autocorrelation-fitting methods don't scale to high-dimensional population recordings and become unreliable when dynamics change. Standard state-space models don't explicitly account for multiple timescales, so they don't guarantee accurate recovery of temporal structure.
AI.method: MTS-SLDS: a switching linear dynamical system framework for regime-specific latent timescales from continuous or spiking observations. It combines a multi-lag moment initialization (capturing temporal structure across observation lags) with regime-conditioned Laplace-EM inference (reducing mixing of dynamical statistics across uncertain regimes). Timescales are extracted from eigenvalues of learned latent transition matrices.
AI.result: In synthetic and neural experiments with Gaussian and Poisson spike observations, MTS-SLDS accurately recovers timescales and switching structure across multiple datasets.
AI.conclusion: MTS-SLDS enables reliable, scalable identification of regime-specific neural timescales from high-dimensional recordings with behavioral/task-dependent dynamics.

title: RipplePLM: Structural and Property Decoupling for Protein Mutation Effect Generation
summary: Protein mutation effect generation asks a model to describe the functional consequence of a point mutation in natural language. Existing protein-to-text systems typically encode mutation information into undifferentiated representations, overlooking the organization of mutation-induced evidence across structural and biochemical factors. We propose RipplePLM, a mutation-aware generation framework centered on Direct-Distal Cross-Attention (DDCA). By constructing a residue-level Mutation Perturbation Field from pre-trained protein language models, DDCA leverages predicted contact maps to organize mutation representations into two pathways: the mutation site's immediate contact neighborhood and its multi-hop distal context. To complement this structural decomposition, we further introduce the Property Latent Chain (PLChain), which injects expert-guided supervision of biochemical property changes (e.g., thermostability and optimal pH) into the LLM hidden-state pathway through latent property tokens. On MutaDescribe, RipplePLM improves over mutation-specific baselines on temporal and structural splits; under a matched-backbone comparison, average structural-split ROUGE-L increases from {22.23} to {35.65}. Expert evaluation further shows a higher proportion of biologically accurate or relevant descriptions than the mutation-specific baseline. Additional ablations, representation diagnostics, and low-$N$ fitness regression experiments further support the effectiveness of the learned mutation-aware representations. Code: https://github.com/Lyu6PosHao/RipplePLM.

AI.tldr: RipplePLM is a mutation-aware protein-to-text framework using Direct-Distal Cross-Attention (DDCA) and Property Latent Chain (PLChain) to generate better descriptions of mutation functional consequences.
AI.motivation: Existing protein-to-text systems encode mutation information into undifferentiated representations, overlooking how mutation-induced evidence is organized across structural and biochemical factors.
AI.method: DDCA builds a residue-level Mutation Perturbation Field from pre-trained protein language models and, using predicted contact maps, splits mutation representations into immediate contact neighborhood and multi-hop distal context. PLChain adds expert-guided biochemical property supervision (e.g., thermostability, optimal pH) into LLM hidden states via latent property tokens.
AI.result: On MutaDescribe, improves over mutation-specific baselines on temporal and structural splits; matched-backbone structural-split ROUGE-L rises from 22.23 to 35.65. Expert evaluation shows more biologically accurate/relevant descriptions. Ablations, representation diagnostics, and low-N fitness regression support the learned representations.
AI.conclusion: Structuring mutation evidence into direct/distal structural pathways plus biochemical property supervision yields more accurate mutation-effect text generation.

title: A foundation for systematic analysis of transformers and RNNs for tractography
summary: Machine learning (ML) has emerged as a promising approach for improving diffusion MRI (dMRI) tractography, a task that remains limited by the intrinsic tension between local diffusion information and global anatomical plausibility. In this work, we systematically evaluate recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and Transformer models for iterative tractography, with particular attention to training strategies, input representations (including convolutional neural network (CNN)-based embeddings and end-of-sequence (EOS) tokens), and hyperparameter selection. We introduce a generation-validation phase enabling supervision at the streamline level during training, allowing supervision despite the mismatch between local loss functions and global streamline quality. Using the ISMRM2015 tractography challenge dataset, our models achieve the highest reported performance to date. Through controlled experiments, we quantify the impact of missing bundles, noisy or imperfect training streamlines, and invalid fibers in the training set. Finally, we demonstrate the applicability of our best-performing models for in vivo data from the Tractoinferno database. Overall, our results highlight both the potential and the limits of sequence-based deep learning models such as Transformers and RNNs for tractography, and emphasize the need for improved phantoms and evaluation methods for in vivo validation. We provide takeaways and recommendations for future researchers training and validating sequence-based supervised methods for tractography.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically evaluates RNNs and Transformers for diffusion MRI tractography, introducing a generation-validation training phase and achieving state-of-the-art results on the ISMRM2015 challenge, while quantifying the effects of training data imperfections.
AI.motivation: dMRI tractography faces an intrinsic tension between local diffusion information and global anatomical plausibility, and existing ML methods lack systematic evaluation of architectures, training strategies, and input representations.
AI.method: The authors evaluate RNNs and Transformers for iterative tractography, examining training strategies, input representations (CNN-based embeddings and EOS tokens), and hyperparameters. They introduce a generation-validation phase for streamline-level supervision.
AI.result: Using the ISMRM2015 tractography challenge dataset, the models achieve the highest reported performance to date. Controlled experiments quantify the impact of missing bundles, noisy/imperfect training streamlines, and invalid fibers, and the best models are applied to in vivo Tractoinferno data.
AI.conclusion: Results highlight both the potential and limits of sequence-based deep learning models for tractography, emphasizing the need for improved phantoms and evaluation methods for in vivo validation, with takeaways for future researchers.

title: Effective Resistance and Graph Neural Network Reliability in Tissue-Specific Interactomes
summary: Protein function annotation needs to know which predictions to distrust, not only what a model predicts. We ask whether tissue-specific interaction structure carries that information. Our candidate signal is effective resistance, used previously to relieve over-squashing by rewiring. Across 24 tissue-specific interactomes it is dominated by inverse degree, and the degeneration deepens as the co-expression filtered network grows, with a Spearman correlation of -0.955. The residual departure from that limit exceeds degree-preserving null graphs in all 24 networks. Controlling for predictive entropy, degree, annotation cardinality, local structure and feature-only difficulty, the residual explains additional per-node loss in 19 of 24 held-out networks once a permutation floor is subtracted, at every depth, and the effect strengthens monotonically with depth. The increment reaches 0.37% of the variance the controls leave unexplained, 5.6 times a permutation floor, against 1.5 times when the model is retrained in a degree-preserving null world. Selective prediction improves negligibly. The signal is reproducible; degree degeneration bounds it.

AI.tldr: Effective resistance in tissue-specific interactomes is largely a restatement of inverse node degree, yet its residual beyond that degeneracy carries reproducible per-node information about where protein function predictions fail, strengthening with model depth.
AI.motivation: Protein function annotation must identify which predictions to distrust, not just what is predicted. The paper asks whether tissue-specific interaction structure encodes that reliability signal, using effective resistance as a candidate.
AI.method: Across 24 tissue-specific interactomes, effective resistance is decomposed into a dominant inverse-degree component and a residual. The residual is tested against degree-preserving null graphs, then used to explain per-node prediction loss while controlling for predictive entropy, degree, annotation cardinality, local structure, and feature-only difficulty, with a permutation floor subtracted, on held-out networks and across model depths.
AI.result: Effective resistance is dominated by inverse degree, with Spearman correlation -0.955 that worsens as the co-expression filtered network grows. The residual exceeds degree-preserving nulls in all 24 networks and explains additional held-out per-node loss in 19 of 24 networks at every depth, strengthening with depth. The increment reaches 0.37% of control-unexplained variance, 5.6x a permutation floor, versus 1.5x when retrained in a degree-preserving null world. Selective prediction gains are negligible.
AI.conclusion: Effective resistance carries a reproducible reliability signal for protein function prediction, but its usefulness is bounded by its degeneration into inverse degree; selective-prediction benefits are negligible.
